Short answer: In NHANES, the crude (unadjusted) correlation between blood lead and hemoglobin in adults is typically weakly positive. After appropriate adjustment (e.g., for sex, age, race/ethnicity, smoking/exposure to CO, iron status, and altitude/hematocrit), the association is near-null to slightly negative, and at higher lead levels the relationship is clearly negative. In children, the association tends to be inverse even with minimal adjustment.

Why this happens despite lead inhibiting heme synthesis:
- Biology of toxicity: Lead inhibits ALAD and ferrochelatase, reducing heme production and, at sufficiently high exposure, lowers hemoglobin (negative association).
- Partitioning/measurement effect: About 95–99% of blood lead is carried in red blood cells. People with higher hematocrit/hemoglobin will, for the same body lead burden, show a higher whole-blood lead concentration—creating a positive correlation unrelated to toxicity.
- Confounding by smoking and hypoxia: Smoking (and other hypoxic stimuli) raises hemoglobin via erythropoiesis and also raises blood lead (tobacco and inhaled particulates), biasing the crude association upward.
- Demographics: Men generally have both higher hemoglobin and higher lead (occupational/behavioral exposures), which also pushes the unadjusted correlation positive.
- Low contemporary exposures: In modern NHANES cycles, most BLLs are low; the heme-synthesis inhibition signal is small and easily masked by the factors above.

Bottom line: The population-level crude correlation in NHANES adults is often positive due to partitioning and confounding, but when you compare like-with-like (non-smokers, same sex/age, similar iron status/altitude), the relationship aligns with biology—near zero to modestly negative, with clearer inverse associations at higher lead levels.
